4.title: Calculate, update and post
4.content: Try measures on the calibrated model, refresh the report with the results, and post it for your contacts and clients. For: AnalyzerTakes: A few minutes per runWhere: Analysis › Energy Audit › ECM Explorer . The baseline is calibrated, pinned and subscribed. See Run an energy audit.

5.title: Steps
5.content: . | In the ECM Explorer, choose the measures you want to apply by changing their values. | Click Calculate. InverseAudit runs the simulation with the selected measures and shows the new savings. The report is marked “The report is outdated”. | If the savings meet your expectations, click Update. The report is updated with the new results. This runs an energy simulation for each measure and can take several minutes. | Optionally, click AI Analyze to rewrite the report’s text with AI. This replaces the text of every report section, including text you edited yourself. | Check the report. If everything is in order, click Post. | .

6.title: When the buttons turn on
6.content: Each time you open the Energy Audit page, Update, AI Analyze and Post start grayed out. | Update turns on when a Calculate finishes. | Post and AI Analyze turn on when an Update finishes. Post also turns on when AI Analyze finishes. | After Unpost, run Calculate and Update again before you can post. | . To post an audit you updated during an earlier visit, run Calculate and Update again.

7.title: What you’ll see next
7.content: Your client can view the posted report (see What clients see), and the building appears on the Dashboard. The Utility analysis tab of the report becomes available. After the audit is posted, Calculate is turned off. To make changes, click Unpost first. Unpost appears only after the audit has been posted.

10.title: Read the calibration results
10.content: How to tell whether the calibrated model is accurate enough, using its goodness of fit. Where: Home › Baseline Controller › Stats and the top of the Benchmark page .

11.title: Goodness of fit
11.content: If a model is calibrated within the threshold limits, it is considered sufficiently accurate in simulating the physical reality it is intended to represent. These thresholds are a preliminary guide for the building calibration and should not be treated as absolute values. The statistical indices here relate only to the predicted building energy consumption. | CV(RMSE) - How much the model’s hourly or monthly values scatter around the measured values. | NMBE - Whether the model uses more or less energy than measured, on average. | .

16.title: Check inputs and run calibration
16.content: The calibration tunes your building’s energy model until it matches your meter data. Every benchmark and audit result comes from the calibrated model. For: AnalyzerTakes: 3 to 40 minutesWhere: Home › Baseline Controller . | All four cards on the baseline are complete: Meter Data, Geometry, Systems and Rates. None shows a Pending badge. | You are the baseline’s analyzer. Other people see the controller in view-only mode. | .

17.title: Steps
17.content: . | On Home, click the baseline’s card. In the Baseline Controller, click Check inputs. The check takes a few seconds and covers your inputs, historical weather data, incentive rates and retrofit costs. Anything that needs fixing is listed on the Issues tab. | When the check passes, the button changes to Run calibration. Choose a Calibration length: . | Quick - About 3 minutes. | Standard - About 20 minutes. Recommended. | Thorough - About 40 minutes. Tests more combinations of model inputs. | . | To get an email when it’s done, check Send me an email when ready. Then click Run calibration and confirm with Run Calibration. | .

18.title: What you’ll see next
18.content: You can leave the page while the calibration runs. The button shows its progress, for example Calibration in progress (45%). When it finishes, it shows Calibration complete, and the Stats tab shows how closely the model matches your meter data: . | Meter data | CV(RMSE) | NMBE | . | Hourly | 30% or less | within ±10% | . | Monthly | 15% or less | within ±5% | . These are the ASHRAE Guideline 14 limits. See Read the calibration results. Next, open Benchmark to see the results. Clicking Calibration complete lets you rerun the calibration. Rerunning deletes the current benchmark and energy audit results, and you’ll need to check inputs and run the calibration again.

19.title: If something goes wrong
19.content: The Check inputs button is grayed out One of the four cards is still incomplete, or you aren’t the baseline’s analyzer. The line under the button says which inputs are missing. I need to stop the calibration Click the progress button and confirm with Stop Calibration. The progress is lost, but your inputs are kept, so you can run it again. If it just started, wait about 10 seconds before stopping it. CV(RMSE) or NMBE is outside the limits Check the meter data for gaps or outliers and confirm the systems and schedules. See Read the calibration results. "Calibration failed" Your inputs are saved. Run the calibration again. If it fails a second time, contact support with the baseline’s name.

34.title: Retrofit costs
34.content: The cost of each measure comes from a retrofit costs table, priced per unit (for example per square foot of roof). Open Dataset › Retrofit Costs in the left menu to see it. When you click Update, the audit prices the measures with your own table for the building’s audit year and state if you have one, and otherwise the Standard dataset. The standard dataset can’t be edited. Calculate only recalculates the savings; the costs, the number of measures and the net project budget are recalculated when you click Update. | Column | Meaning | . | Life Expectancy | Years the measure lasts. Used for the SIR. | . | Bare Material | Material cost per unit, without overhead and profit | . | Bare Labor | Labor cost per unit, without overhead and profit | . | Bare Total Costs | Bare material + bare labor | . | Multiplier | Overhead and profit markup. A blank multiplier counts as 1. | . | Total O&P | Bare Total Costs × Multiplier, the cost per unit used in the audit | . Create your own costs table . | On Retrofit Costs, click NEW COSTS TABLE. | Choose the audit year and state the table is for. | Choose Copy from a standard dataset, Copy from your dataset or Create an empty dataset, and click Create Table. | Edit the costs, then click Save changes. The bare total and Total O&P columns update when the page reloads. | . Each year and state can have one table. Make the table for the building’s own state, because the audit only picks up a table whose state matches the building. Change the cost of one measure . On the Recommendations tab of the report, the analyzer can click a measure’s Retrofit Costs or Utility Incentives value, enter a new amount and click Update. A retrofit cost you type in is kept the next time you update the report. All other costs are priced again from the current retrofit costs table.

35.title: Utility incentives
35.content: Open Dataset › Utility Incentives and choose the Utility, Service Rate and Audit Year to see the incentive programs InverseAudit knows about. This page is maintained by InverseAudit. If your utility’s programs are missing or out of date, click Contact Us. | Performance-based incentives pay per kWh and per kW saved. These are the ones the audit calculates. | Retrofit-based incentives are listed with their program name and website for reference. They aren’t added to the audit’s totals. | The Whole building tab holds programs that pay for the whole building’s savings or per square foot. | . Incentives need a utility rate. With an average rate, the Net project budget card says that incentives can’t be applied. See Rates. In the Energy Audit, the Net project budget card shows the retrofit cost after incentives. Under its Manage menu, the analyzer chooses the Incentive Method: Measure-based or Whole building. Only methods the utility offers can be chosen. The Dashboard and the report use the same method. Whole-building incentives add the Performance row (per kWh and kW saved) and the Building Area row (per ft²) when their switches are on. When the program sets a Max Limit (%), the building-area part is limited to that share of the project budget.

36.title: Payback and SIR
36.content: | Value | Formula | Where | . | Payback period | Cost of measures ÷ annual cost savings | Payback period card, Summary tab | . | Net payback period | (Cost of measures − incentives) ÷ annual cost savings | Summary tab, when there are incentives | . | SIR | Annual cost savings × life expectancy ÷ (retrofit cost − incentive) | Recommendations tab | . Savings aren’t discounted. An SIR above 1 means the measure pays for itself over its life. A payback under 30 years shows a green flag on the card. The Summary tab shows the savings of all selected measures implemented together. The Recommendations tab shows each measure on its own, so its rows don’t add up to the summary.

38.title: Create a baseline
38.content: A baseline holds your building’s information and data, and becomes its calibrated energy model. For: Anyone with an accountTakes: 2 minutesWhere: Home › Baselines . Have the building’s full postal address ready, and know whether your electricity data is hourly (interval) or monthly. See What you need.

39.title: Steps
39.content: . | On Home, open the Baselines tab and click Create Baseline. | In the Building Information window, enter a building name, the year built and a description. You can also assign a client. A baseline that isn’t assigned to a client isn’t visible to clients. | Enter the building’s full postal address. InverseAudit uses it to find the building’s footprint on the map and to pick the weather data for the calibration. | Under Electric Meter Data Type, choose Hourly if you have interval data (15-, 30- or 60-minute) or Monthly if you have utility bills. Interval data gives a more accurate model. | Click Create. | .

40.content: The baselines you’re working on appear on the Home tab under Pinned Baselines. Use the Pin switch on the Baselines tab to pin or unpin a baseline. Benchmark and Energy Audit list only pinned baselines, and the Dashboard shows only pinned baselines with a posted audit. Each pinned baseline has four cards to complete: Meter Data, Geometry, Systems and Rates. A card shows an orange Pending badge until its data is saved.

41.title: Change the building information
41.content: Open the ⋮ menu on the baseline’s card and choose Edit Building Info, or click Edit next to the baseline on the Baselines tab. The window shows Interval data and Monthly data in place of Hourly and Monthly, and Save changes in place of Create. Changing the postal code or the electric meter data type marks the Meter Data and Systems cards incomplete again, and a calibrated baseline goes back to preparation.

48.title: Electricity
48.content: kW and kWh in interval meter data . Interval meter data typically presents energy consumption information in two key metrics: kilowatts (kW) and kilowatt-hours (kWh). Proper interpretation of these metrics is crucial for accurate energy analysis and billing. Definitions . | kW (kilowatt): A measure of power, representing the rate of energy consumption at a given moment. | kWh (kilowatt-hour): A measure of energy, representing the total amount of electricity consumed over a period of time. | . Data conversion . When converting interval data to hourly figures: . | kW values are averaged to represent the mean power demand. | kWh values are summed to represent the total energy consumption. | . Critical Interpretation . Misinterpreting kW as kWh or vice versa can lead to significant errors in energy calculations: . | If 30-minute kW intervals are treated as kWh, annual energy consumption is overestimated by 100% (double the actual kWh). | If 30-minute kWh intervals are treated as kW, annual energy consumption is underestimated by 50% (half the actual kWh). | . These errors, when propagated over extended periods, can result in substantial discrepancies in energy analysis. Data formats for InverseAudit . InverseAudit supports two major data formats: Green Button and CSV. This manual outlines the specifications for each format and how they are handled by the system. Green Button format . The Green Button is a standardized data format designed for easy and secure access to energy usage data. | Format: Standardized, machine-readable | Purpose: Allows utility customers to access their energy usage data in a consumer-friendly format | Handling: InverseAudit consumes Green Button data without any modification | . CSV (comma-separated values) format . CSV is a common output format for spreadsheet programs. InverseAudit supports two types of CSV formats and can automatically recognize the type. Horizontal CSV format . | Structure: Horizontal header shows time, First column shows date | Default Unit: kW | Unit Specification: If needed, include “kWh” or “kW” in the first cell of the first column | File Extension: .csv | . Vertical CSV format . InverseAudit supports two variations of the vertical format: . Two-column format . | Column 1: Date and time combined | Column 2: Electricity usage data | . Three-column format . | Column 1: Date | Column 2: Time | Column 3: Electricity usage data | . Data import process . InverseAudit automatically detects the format of the imported file (Green Button or CSV). For CSV files, the system determines whether it’s a horizontal or vertical format. The data is then processed according to the identified format. Best practices . | Keep the data consistent within each file. | For CSV files, keep the structure described above. | With the horizontal CSV format, specify the unit (kW or kWh) if it differs from the default. | .

83.title: Terms
83.content: . | Analyzer: The person who enters the baseline’s data, runs the calibration and performs the energy audit. Other people the baseline is shared with see it in view-only mode. See Roles and the analyzer. | ASHRAE Guideline 14: A guideline for measuring energy savings. Its CV(RMSE) and NMBE limits are used to judge whether a calibrated model fits the meter data. | ASHRAE Level 2 audit: An energy survey and analysis that identifies energy conservation measures with their savings and cost estimates. | Asset gap: The energy a building uses above the code-compliant scenario because of its design, envelope and equipment (B - C). | Asset score: A rating of a building’s as-built physical characteristics and energy systems, independent of occupancy and operation. It compares the calibrated model with the same building built to the selected energy code: 100 - 50 × A / C. | Audit report: The report produced on the Energy Audit page, with the Summary, Analysis, Recommendations and Utility analysis tabs. It can be downloaded as PDF. | Average rate: A single rate per unit of energy, used when your utility’s rate structure isn’t selected. With an average rate, demand cost savings and utility incentives aren’t calculated. Also called a blended rate. | Baseline: Your building in InverseAudit: its information, meter data, geometry, systems and rates, and the energy model calibrated from them. | Calibration: The process that tunes the building’s energy model until it matches the meter data. See Check inputs and run calibration. | Calibration length: How long the calibration searches for the best fit: Quick (about 3 minutes), Standard (about 20 minutes, recommended) or Thorough (about 40 minutes). | Client: A company you share audits with. Its contacts sign in with I’m reviewing an audit report and see the posted audits of baselines assigned to the company. | Climate zone: A geographic region defined by ASHRAE standards, characterized by similar weather patterns, used to determine the energy code requirements. | Compared scenarios (A, B, C): The three versions of the building used on the Benchmark page, all derived from the calibrated model. A is the building as it operates today, B is the same building with typical schedules and setpoints, and C is the same building built to the selected energy code. | CV(RMSE): A statistical measure of how much the model’s results vary from the measured data: the root mean squared error divided by the mean of the measured data. A lower value means a better fit. ASHRAE Guideline 14 accepts up to 30% for hourly data and 15% for monthly data. | End-use analysis: A breakdown of energy use by category within a building, such as lighting, heating, cooling or plug loads. | Energy conservation measure (ECM): A specific action or upgrade that reduces a building’s energy use or improves its efficiency. | Energy use gap: How much more energy the building uses than the code-compliant scenario (A - C), split into the asset gap and the operational gap. See Scenarios and the energy use gap. | Energy use intensity (EUI): A building’s annual energy use divided by its floor area, usually in kBtu/ft². | ENERGY STAR score: A 1-100 rating of a building’s energy efficiency compared with similar buildings nationwide. Higher is better, and 50 is the median. | Green Button: A standardized XML format for downloading energy use data from a utility. | Interval data: Meter data recorded every 15, 30 or 60 minutes, usually by a smart meter or a BEMS. | Lighting power density: Installed lighting power per floor area, in W/ft². | Net payback period: The cost of the measures minus incentives, divided by the annual cost savings. | NMBE: A statistical measure of the model’s overall bias: the mean difference between measured and simulated data, divided by the mean of the measured data. A value closer to zero is better. ASHRAE Guideline 14 accepts within ±10% for hourly data and ±5% for monthly data. | Operational gap: The energy a building uses above the typical operation scenario because of its schedules, setpoints and operating practice (A - B). | Operational score: A rating of how the building is operated. It compares the calibrated model with the same building run on typical (ASHRAE) schedules: 100 - 50 × A / B. | Payback period: The time it takes for a measure’s savings to equal its cost. | Performance-based incentive: A utility incentive paid per kWh and per kW saved. | Post / Unpost: Posting shares the audit report with the baseline’s client and adds the building to the Dashboard. Unposting hides the report again so you can make changes. | R-value: A material’s thermal resistance, in ft²·h·°F/Btu. Higher is better insulated. | Savings-to-investment ratio (SIR): A measure’s savings over its lifetime divided by its net cost (retrofit cost minus incentives). InverseAudit doesn’t discount future savings. | Setback temperature: A less strict temperature setting used during unoccupied periods to save energy while keeping minimal comfort. | Setpoint temperature: The temperature the HVAC system maintains during occupied periods. | Site EUI: The energy used on site per floor area, in kBtu/ft² per year. | Source EUI: Site energy plus the losses from producing and delivering it, per floor area. ENERGY STAR uses source energy. | Subscriber: The baseline’s owner: the person who created it, or the new owner after a transfer. The subscriber subscribes and cancels, and assigns the analyzer. | U-value: The rate of heat transfer through a building element, in Btu/h·ft²·°F. Lower is better insulated. | Weather normalization: Adjusting energy use for weather, so different periods or locations can be compared fairly. | Whole-building energy model: A simulation of the building’s energy performance as one system, including climate, envelope and mechanical systems. | .

84.content: The models behind the benchmark scores and the energy savings. On this page . | Calibrated model | Weather-normalized model | Two reference models . | Operational score | Asset score | . | Energy savings | Related | .

85.title: Calibrated model
85.content: . | What it is: A model based on actual weather data and measured energy use. | How it’s used: The starting point for all other calculations. | .

86.title: Weather-normalized model
86.content: . | What it is: The calibrated model run with typical weather data (TMY3). | How it’s used: For consistent energy analysis across different time periods. | .

87.title: Two reference models
87.content: The scores compare your building with two versions of itself: . | Typical Operation Scenario (B) - Your building with standard (ASHRAE) operating schedules and setpoints. It shows how much of your energy use comes from how the building is operated. | Code-Compliant Scenario (C) - Your building built to just meet the selected energy code. It shows how much comes from the building itself: its envelope and equipment. | . On the Benchmark page, your building as it operates today is the Current Building Performance (A). Both scores use a scale where 100 means using no energy and 50 means using exactly as much as the reference scenario. Higher is better. Operational score . | Reference: Typical Operation Scenario (B), using standard (ASHRAE) schedules instead of the actual operating conditions | Formula: Operational score = 100 - 50 × A EUI / B EUI | . Asset score . | Reference: Code-Compliant Scenario (C), with the input parameters changed to meet the selected energy code | Formula: Asset score = 100 - 50 × A EUI / C EUI | .

145.title: ENERGY STAR score
145.content: The ENERGY STAR score rates your building’s overall energy performance on a 1 to 100 scale, reflecting its physical assets, how it’s operated and how it’s used. A score of 50 is the median: lower is worse than similar buildings nationwide, and higher is better. It helps you decide which buildings to improve first.1 . The card shows your building’s score and site EUI next to the portfolio median (a score of 50) and its site EUI. The site EUI uses the modeled floor area, so it matches the calibrated model. If the model changes, for example after you rerun the calibration, the score is recalculated the next time you open the page. To calculate the score for a different property type, choose it under Select Building Type and click the refresh button next to it. Some building types aren’t covered by ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, and no score is shown for them.

146.title: Operational and asset scores
146.content: The operational score and the asset score work like the ENERGY STAR score: 50 means the same energy use as the reference, a lower score is worse, and a higher score is better. Both compare your building with a version of itself rather than with other buildings. | Operational score - Compares the calibrated model with the same building run on typical schedules based on ASHRAE standards. For example, if an office building runs longer than the typical Monday to Friday, 8 am to 5 pm schedule, its operational score is lower than 50. Operational score = 100 - 50 × A / B | Asset score - Similar to the miles-per-gallon (MPG) rating used for cars. It compares the calibrated model with the same building built to the selected energy code (ASHRAE Standard 90.1): roof and exterior wall insulation, window U-values and SHGC, and heating and cooling efficiencies. Asset score = 100 - 50 × A / C | . A, B and C are the three compared scenarios. Scores range from 0 to 100. The scores are calculated with weather-normalized models, which use typical weather (TMY3) in place of the actual weather data. See How scores are calculated.

147.title: Energy cost vs. energy code
147.content: Current Performance vs. Energy Code shows how much higher or lower your building’s energy cost is than the code-compliant scenario, and how the current energy cost is split between energy sources. To compare with a different code, click the energy code’s name and choose another one. The results are recalculated, which can take up to 10 seconds. The code currently in force in your state is tagged Current State Code. Only the baseline’s analyzer can change the code.

170.title: What InverseAudit does
170.content: InverseAudit is an energy auditing platform for commercial buildings. It builds a calibrated energy model of your building from monthly or interval meter data, without the effort that manual modeling and calibration require.

171.title: The workflow
171.content: graph LR A["Create a baseline"] --> B["Enter data"] B --> C["Calibrate"] C --> D["Benchmark"] D --> E["Subscribe"] E --> F["Energy audit"] F --> G["Post the report"] . | Create a baseline for your building. | Enter its meter data, geometry, systems and rates. | Run the calibration. InverseAudit tunes the model until it matches your meter data. | Review the benchmark results. | Subscribe the baseline to unlock the energy audit. | In the energy audit, try energy conservation measures and see their savings and payback. | Post the report so your contacts and clients can see it. | .

172.title: Why a model should be calibrated
172.content: Energy modeling is not always accurate, especially for older existing buildings. A model’s accuracy is limited by the complexity of buildings. It also depends on operational factors such as schedules and occupancy, how systems and equipment are operated, plug loads and weather.1 A model that hasn’t been calibrated with utility data isn’t accurate, so it should be calibrated before energy cost savings are calculated.

173.title: Why use InverseAudit
173.content: . | It creates and calibrates a model based on your utility data and historical weather data. This leads to an accurate and representative model of your building. | You can perform an energy audit equivalent to an ASHRAE Level 2 energy audit. | . InverseAudit can be used for: . | ASHRAE Level 2 energy audits | Building Energy Ordinance programs | LEED O+M: Existing Buildings | .

174.title: Methodologies and standards
174.content: InverseAudit incorporates industry standards such as: . | ASHRAE Standard 90.1 | ASHRAE Standard 211 | IPMVP (International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol) | . It combines them with its own calibration methods. See How scores are calculated for the models behind the results. To try it, follow the Quick start with the Demo Building. | How Accurate is Energy Modeling in the Market. ↩ . | .
